criteria.description: Correctly identifies the gain: much cheaper per-step cost, more steps in the same time.
Correctly identifies the cost: noisy, unbiased-but-not-exact gradient estimates per step.

commonErrors: Saying SGD is 'always better' or 'always worse' without articulating the actual tradeoff.
Not mentioning the unbiasedness (correct on average) property of the mini-batch estimate.

solutions.fullSolution: You gain speed: each step only touches a small mini-batch instead of all N data points, so each step is far cheaper, letting you take many more steps in the same wall-clock time, which matters enormously when N is large. You give up per-step accuracy: a mini-batch's average gradient is a noisy estimate of the true full-batch gradient, correct only on average (unbiased) across many different random mini-batches, not exactly equal to the true gradient on any single step. In practice, for large datasets, trading per-step accuracy for many more (cheap) steps usually wins, since the noise tends to average out over the course of optimization.

Mini-batch gradient estimate using {3,4}: (1/2)[(0-3)+(0-4)] = (1/2)(-7) = -3.5. x1 = x0 - alpha * (-3.5) = 0 - 0.2*(-3.5) = 0.7. (For comparison, the true full-batch gradient using all 5 points is -3, so the mini-batch estimate of -3.5 is noisy but in the right ballpark, illustrating the tradeoff from the previous exercise.)

criteria.description: Correctly substitutes w_{k+1}-w_k = -alpha_k*grad f_i(w_k) into the quadratic upper bound.
Correctly takes expectations and uses unbiasedness E{grad f_i(w_k)}=grad f(w_k) to simplify the cross term to ||grad f(w_k)||^2.

commonErrors: Forgetting that grad f(w_k) itself is a fixed (non-random) quantity given w_k, so it can be pulled out of the expectation over the random index i.

solutions.fullSolution:
Substituting w=w_{k+1}, w-bar=w_k, w-w-bar = -alpha_k*grad f_i(w_k) into f(w) <= f(w-bar) + grad f(w-bar)^T(w-w-bar) + (L/2)||w-w-bar||^2:
f(w_{k+1}) <= f(w_k) + grad f(w_k)^T(-alpha_k grad f_i(w_k)) + (L/2)||alpha_k grad f_i(w_k)||^2
= f(w_k) - alpha_k * grad f(w_k)^T grad f_i(w_k) + (1/2)alpha_k^2 L ||grad f_i(w_k)||^2.
Taking expectations (over the random sample i, given w_k fixed): E{grad f(w_k)^T grad f_i(w_k)} = grad f(w_k)^T E{grad f_i(w_k)} = grad f(w_k)^T grad f(w_k) = ||grad f(w_k)||^2 (using unbiasedness of the mini-batch gradient estimator, and that grad f(w_k) is a constant given w_k).
So E{f(w_{k+1})} <= f(w_k) - alpha_k ||grad f(w_k)||^2 + (1/2)alpha_k^2 L E{||grad f_i(w_k)||^2}, exactly as claimed.

criteria.description: Correctly computes m_hat_1 and shows the (1-beta_1) factors cancel exactly, giving m_hat_1=g_1.

solutions.fullSolution:
m_1 = beta_1*m_0 + (1-beta_1)*g_1 = beta_1*0 + (1-beta_1)*g_1 = (1-beta_1)*g_1.
m_hat_1 = m_1/(1-beta_1^1) = (1-beta_1)*g_1 / (1-beta_1) = g_1 (the (1-beta_1) factors cancel exactly, for any beta_1 != 1).
Without bias correction, m_1=(1-beta_1)*g_1 would badly underestimate g_1 for beta_1 close to 1 (e.g. beta_1=0.9 gives m_1=0.1*g_1, a 10x underestimate); the correction removes this bias completely at t=1, and progressively less aggressively as t grows (since beta_1^t -> 0).

criteria.description: Correctly notes NFL's averaging is over ALL possible functions, including structureless/adversarial ones that never arise in practice.
Correctly connects this to: specialized methods work by exploiting real structure present in actual problems, which is exactly what NFL doesn't rule out.

commonErrors: Concluding NFL means optimization method choice doesn't matter in practice (missing the key distinction between 'all possible functions' and 'the structured functions that actually arise').
Not identifying WHAT structure the specialized methods actually exploit (smoothness, local curvature, convexity, etc.).

solutions.fullSolution: NFL's averaging is over the space of ALL conceivable objective functions, including wildly adversarial, discontinuous, or effectively random ones where knowing f at one point tells you nothing about f nearby. Real optimization problems (robot dynamics costs, training losses, physical systems) are never drawn uniformly from that space; they have real structure: smoothness (so Taylor expansions are valid), often local or global convexity, gradients that genuinely correlate with nearby behavior. The specialized methods in this course (Newton, Gauss-Newton, SGD, etc.) work precisely because they exploit that structure. NFL says there's no single method that's simultaneously good at exploiting structure on structured problems AND good on structureless adversarial ones; it does NOT say structure-exploiting methods are useless on the structured problems that actually show up in practice, which is nearly everything you'll ever optimize.
